subject: music
topicDisplay: Area of Study 2: The Concerto Through Time
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a concerto?
options: A work for solo instrument(s) contrasted with an orchestra
A work for solo keyboard only
A dance suite for full orchestra
questions.explain: A concerto sets one or more solo instruments against the orchestra, exploiting the contrast between them.

questions.q: In a Baroque concerto grosso, what is the small group of soloists called?
questions.explain: The concertino is the small group of soloists that contrasts with the full ensemble.

questions.q: In a concerto grosso, what name is given to the full orchestra or tutti section?
questions.explain: The ripieno (or tutti) is the full body of players that alternates with the concertino.

questions.q: Which Baroque composer wrote The Four Seasons?
questions.explain: Vivaldi composed The Four Seasons, among the most famous of all Baroque concertos.

questions.q: The Four Seasons is best described as a set of concertos for which solo instrument?
questions.explain: The Four Seasons is a set of four violin concertos, each depicting a season.

questions.q: Which keyboard instrument typically played the basso continuo in a Baroque concerto?
questions.explain: The harpsichord commonly realised the basso continuo, filling in the harmony in Baroque music.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of ritornello form, common in Baroque concerto movements?
options: A recurring tutti theme alternates with contrasting solo episodes
A single theme is developed in a fugue
Two themes are stated in a double exposition
A theme returns with a new melody each time in a rondo
questions.explain: In ritornello form the orchestral ritornello keeps returning between passages for the soloist(s).

questions.q: J. S. Bach's celebrated set of six concertos is known as the:
questions.explain: The Brandenburg Concertos are six works by Bach, several in concerto grosso style.

questions.q: What is the usual order of movements in a three-movement concerto?
questions.explain: The standard concerto plan is a fast first movement, a lyrical slow movement, and a lively finale.

questions.q: Which Classical composer is especially renowned for his many piano concertos?
questions.explain: Mozart wrote a large and influential body of piano concertos in the Classical period.

questions.q: What is a cadenza in a concerto?
options: A virtuosic passage, often unaccompanied, that displays the soloist's skill
A closing chord progression for the whole orchestra
questions.explain: A cadenza lets the soloist show off technically, usually with the orchestra silent.

questions.q: The first movement of a Classical concerto is typically built on:
options: Sonata form with a double exposition
questions.explain: Classical first movements use sonata form, with the orchestra and then the soloist each presenting the exposition.

questions.q: As the concerto developed, which instrument gradually replaced the harpsichord as the main keyboard soloist?
questions.explain: The piano, with its wider dynamic range, superseded the harpsichord from the Classical period onwards.

questions.q: Compared with a Baroque concerto, a Romantic concerto typically features:
options: Greater virtuosity, a larger orchestra and more expressive writing
A smaller ensemble and continuo throughout
Strict terraced dynamics and no cadenza
questions.explain: Romantic concertos exploit a bigger orchestra, extreme soloist virtuosity and heightened emotional expression.

questions.q: Which Romantic violinist-composer became legendary for his extreme virtuosity, writing works such as the 24 Caprices?
questions.explain: Paganini was a Romantic virtuoso whose demanding violin writing pushed technique to new limits.

questions.q: You hear a lyrical, dramatic Romantic concerto for solo piano and large orchestra, opening with a famous descending piano flourish, by a Norwegian composer. This is most likely by:
questions.explain: Grieg's Piano Concerto in A minor is a well-known Romantic concerto with its striking opening piano flourish.

questions.q: 'Terraced dynamics', typical of Baroque concertos, means:
options: Sudden shifts between loud and soft rather than gradual changes
A slow crescendo across a whole movement
questions.explain: Terraced dynamics move abruptly between dynamic levels, a hallmark of Baroque style.

questions.q: You hear a work in which two solo violins and a cello are set against a full string orchestra with harpsichord continuo, using sudden dynamic changes. This is most likely a:
questions.explain: A small solo group (concertino) contrasting with a string ripieno plus continuo is characteristic of the Baroque concerto grosso.

questions.q: Near the end of a concerto's first movement, the orchestra falls silent while the soloist plays an elaborate, showy passage alone. This is a:
questions.explain: An unaccompanied virtuosic passage for the soloist within a movement is a cadenza.

questions.q: You hear a single virtuoso pianist against a very large orchestra, with rich harmonies, expressive rubato and sweeping emotion. This concerto most likely dates from which period?
questions.explain: A large orchestra, intense virtuosity, rubato and heightened emotion are typical of the Romantic concerto.
